paragraphs: The rest of the argument against the Constitution's provisions on taxation is grafted onto the following clause. The last clause of the eighth section of the first article of the plan under consideration authorizes the national legislature "to make all laws which shall be NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying into execution THE POWERS by that Constitution vested in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof." And the second clause of the sixth article declares "that the Constitution and the laws of the United States made IN PURSUANCE THEREOF, and the treaties made by their authority shall be the SUPREME LAW of the land, any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."

These two clauses have been the source of much bitter invective and petulant declamation against the proposed Constitution. They have been held up to the people, in all the exaggerated colors of misrepresentation, as the destructive engines by which their local governments were to be destroyed and their liberties wiped out. They have been called a hideous monster whose devouring jaws would spare neither sex nor age, neither high nor low, neither sacred nor profane. And yet, strange as it may appear after all this clamor, anyone who has not happened to look at them in the same light may be told with perfect confidence that the constitutional operation of the intended government would be precisely the same if these clauses were entirely struck out as if they were repeated in every article. They only declare a truth that would have followed by necessary and unavoidable implication from the very act of constituting a federal government and vesting it with certain specified powers. This proposition is so clear that even moderation itself can scarcely listen to the railings so copiously poured out against this part of the plan without emotions that disturb its calm.

What is a power, but the ability or faculty of doing a thing? What is the ability to do a thing, but the power of employing the MEANS necessary to carry it out? What is a LEGISLATIVE power, but a power of making LAWS? What are the MEANS of carrying out a LEGISLATIVE power, but LAWS? What is the power of laying and collecting taxes, but a LEGISLATIVE POWER, or a power of MAKING LAWS to lay and collect taxes? What are the proper means of carrying out such a power, but NECESSARY and PROPER laws?

This simple train of inquiry gives us at once a test by which to judge the true nature of the clause complained of. It leads us to this plain truth: a power to lay and collect taxes must be a power to pass all laws NECESSARY and PROPER for the execution of that power. And what does the unfortunate and slandered provision in question do more than declare the same truth, namely that the national legislature, to whom the power of laying and collecting taxes had previously been given, might, in the execution of that power, pass all laws NECESSARY and PROPER to carry it into effect? I have applied these observations particularly to the power of taxation because it is the subject immediately under consideration, and because it is the most important of the authorities proposed to be conferred upon the Union. But the same process will lead to the same result in regard to all the other powers declared in the Constitution. And it is EXPRESSLY to carry out these powers that the sweeping clause, as it has been affectedly called, authorizes the national legislature to pass all NECESSARY and PROPER laws. If anything in it is objectionable, the objection must be sought in the specific powers on which this general declaration rests. The declaration itself, though it may be charged with tautology or redundancy, is at least perfectly harmless.

But SUSPICION may ask: why, then, was it introduced? The answer is that it could only have been done out of greater caution, and to guard against all quibbling refinements by those who might hereafter feel inclined to curtail and evade the legitimate authorities of the Union. The Convention probably foresaw what it has been a principal aim of these papers to impress, that the danger which most threatens our political welfare is that the State governments will finally undermine the foundations of the Union. It might therefore have thought it necessary, on so cardinal a point, to leave nothing to construction. Whatever the reason for including it, the wisdom of the precaution is evident from the outcry raised against it, since that very outcry betrays a disposition to question the great and essential truth which it is manifestly the object of that provision to declare.

But it may be asked again: who is to judge of the NECESSITY and PROPRIETY of the laws to be passed for carrying out the powers of the Union? I answer, first, that this question arises as fully on the simple grant of those powers as on the declaratory clause. I answer, in the second place, that the national government, like every other, must judge in the first instance of the proper exercise of its powers, and its constituents in the last. If the federal government should overstep the just bounds of its authority and make a tyrannical use of its powers, the people, whose creature it is, must appeal to the standard they have formed, and take such measures to redress the injury done to the Constitution as the emergency may suggest and prudence justify. The propriety of a law, in a constitutional light, must always be determined by the nature of the powers on which it is founded. Suppose that, by some forced construction of its authority (which indeed cannot easily be imagined), the federal legislature should attempt to change the law of descent in any State. Would it not be evident that, in making such an attempt, it had exceeded its jurisdiction and infringed upon that of the State? Suppose again that, on the pretense of an interference with its revenues, it should undertake to abolish a land tax imposed by the authority of a State. Would it not be equally evident that this was an invasion of that concurrent jurisdiction in this kind of tax which the Constitution plainly supposes to exist in the State governments? If a doubt on this point should ever arise, the blame for it will be entirely due to those reasoners who, in the imprudent zeal of their hostility to the plan of the Convention, have labored to wrap it in a cloud calculated to obscure the plainest and simplest truths.

But it is said that the laws of the Union are to be the SUPREME LAW of the land. What inference can be drawn from this? What would those laws amount to if they were not supreme? It is evident they would amount to nothing. A LAW, by the very meaning of the term, includes supremacy. It is a rule that those to whom it is prescribed are bound to observe. This results from every political association. If individuals enter into a state of society, the laws of that society must be the supreme regulator of their conduct. If a number of political societies enter into a larger political society, the laws which the latter may enact, in accordance with the powers entrusted to it by its constitution, must necessarily be supreme over those societies and over the individuals of whom they are composed. Otherwise it would be a mere treaty, dependent on the good faith of the parties, and not a government, which is only another word for POLITICAL POWER AND SUPREMACY. But it will not follow from this doctrine that acts of the larger society which are NOT PURSUANT to its constitutional powers, but which are invasions of the residuary authorities of the smaller societies, will become the supreme law of the land. These will be merely acts of usurpation, and will deserve to be treated as such. We therefore see that the clause declaring the supremacy of the laws of the Union, like the one we have just considered, only declares a truth which flows immediately and necessarily from the institution of a federal government. It will not, I presume, have escaped notice that it EXPRESSLY confines this supremacy to laws made PURSUANT TO THE CONSTITUTION. I mention this merely as an instance of caution on the part of the Convention, since that limitation would have been understood even if it had not been expressed.

Therefore, although a law laying a tax for the use of the United States would be supreme in its nature and could not legally be opposed or controlled, a law abolishing or preventing the collection of a tax laid by the authority of a State (unless on imports and exports) would not be the supreme law of the land, but a usurpation of power not granted by the Constitution. To the extent that an improper accumulation of taxes on the same object might make collection difficult or uncertain, this would be a problem for both sides. It would arise not from superior or defective power on either side, but from an unwise exercise of power by one or the other, in a manner equally disadvantageous to both. It is to be hoped and presumed, however, that mutual interest would dictate a coordination in this respect that would avoid any serious problem. The inference from the whole is that the individual States would, under the proposed Constitution, retain an independent and uncontrollable authority to raise revenue to any extent they may need, by every kind of taxation except duties on imports and exports. It will be shown in the next paper that this CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in the matter of taxation was the only admissible substitute for an entire subordination of State authority to that of the Union in this branch of power.
